extracted_claims.text: Under Article 43, providers of high-risk AI systems must follow either the internal control procedure in Annex VI or the assessment procedure involving a notified body in Annex VII, with Annex VII required where harmonised standards do not exist or compliance with them is only partial, or for the specific case of Annex III point 1 (biometrics) systems.
Providers of high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometrics) may choose between internal control (Annex VI) or involving a notified body for conformity assessment (Annex VII).

For the conformity assessment procedure under Annex VII, the provider may choose any notified body, except where the system is intended to be put into service by law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities or by Union institutions, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority (Article 74(8) or (9)) acts as the notified body.

The AI Act establishes a notification and designation system for conformity assessment bodies under Chapter III, Section 4 (Articles 28–35), covering notifying authorities, application and notification procedures, requirements for notified bodies, subsidiaries/subcontracting, operational obligations, and identification numbers/lists.

Notified bodies and their designations are published and tracked via the Commission's NANDO (New Approach Notified and Designated Organisations) information system, which is the authoritative electronic register.
The Commission may adopt delegated acts under Article 43(5) to update Annex VI and Annex VII conformity assessment procedures in light of technical progress.

As of early-to-mid 2026, very few notified bodies have been formally designated specifically for AI Act conformity assessment; existing notified bodies under other product legislation (e.g., MDR, Machinery Regulation) can assess AI components within their existing scope, but AI-specific designation remains limited.

As of September 2026, the pool of AI Act notified bodies is still forming, and providers using the Annex VII route are advised to engage candidate bodies early due to lead-time issues similar to those seen with ISO/IEC 42001 certification.

Industry commentary notes the AI Act notified-body designation bottleneck mirrors capacity shortages seen after the rollout of the Medical Device Regulation (MDR) and In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR).

Germany's draft KI-MIG law designates the Bundesnetzagentur as the notifying authority for AI Act notified bodies, with DAkkS supporting accreditation; established bodies such as TÜV and DEKRA entities are expected to seek AI Act designation.

Ireland's Statutory Instrument No. 366 of 2025 implemented a decentralised model with 15 existing bodies designated as market surveillance authorities; a National AI Office is expected to be established in Ireland by 2 August 2026 as the central coordinating authority.

Proposed amendments under discussion (Digital Omnibus-related Council documents) reference facilitating the designation of notified bodies for AI systems also covered by Medical Devices (MD) or In Vitro Diagnostic Medical Devices (IVDM) regulations, noting two existing NANDO codes for MD and IVD notified bodies.
A Council/Commission document proposes amendments empowering the AI Office in relation to NANDO and related engines.
The original AI Act text set 2 August 2026 as the application date for high-risk obligations tied to Annex III, including conformity assessment requirements.

The European Commission's November 2025 Digital Omnibus proposal sought to delay the Annex III high-risk compliance deadline (including conformity assessment and CE marking) from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027 (a 16-month deferral), citing the late arrival of harmonized technical standards and lack of designated notified bodies as the reason.

As of a Cloud Security Alliance research note, the Digital Omnibus delay proposal had not yet been enacted into law, and enterprises were advised to treat 2 August 2026 as the operative deadline for Articles 9–17 and Article 26 obligations.

According to Foundational.io and Cooley/JDSupra, the Digital Omnibus on AI became binding law as of the week of 10 July 2026, pushing the high-risk Annex III conformity assessment and CE marking deadline from August 2026 to December 2027, with the deadline for Annex I product-embedded high-risk systems moved from 2 August 2027 to 2 August 2028.

The Digital Omnibus amendment allows conformity assessment bodies to submit applications for AI Act designation at any time during and after an 18-month period starting 27 July 2026, without prejudice to Article 28 notification procedures.

Prohibited AI practices under Article 5 became enforceable in February 2025, and GPAI model obligations (Articles 51-55) took effect in August 2025, separate from the high-risk Annex III conformity assessment timeline.

contradictions.description: Sources disagree on whether the Digital Omnibus delay to the high-risk/Annex III conformity assessment deadline had been formally adopted into law; source 38 treats it as merely proposed and not yet binding, while sources 36, 39, 40, and 42 describe it as enacted/binding law with a new December 2027 deadline.

contradictions.claim_a: Providers of high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometrics) must choose between internal control or involving a notified body for conformity assessment.
contradictions.claim_b: The provider shall follow the Annex VII (notified body) conformity assessment procedure where harmonised standards do not exist and common specifications are lacking, implying Annex VI is not always an available choice for all systems, including possibly biometric systems depending on standards availability.
contradictions.description: There is tension/ambiguity between sources describing Annex III point 1 (biometric) systems as always having a choice between Annex VI and Annex VII (source 2) versus other sources indicating the Annex VII route becomes mandatory when harmonised standards are unavailable, which some sources (33) suggest is currently the case for biometric systems, making the 'choice' potentially illusory in practice.

open_issues: No source provides a definitive, current, comprehensive list of specific notified bodies that have been designated and listed in NANDO specifically for AI Act conformity assessment as of October 2026.

It is unclear from the sources exactly how many notified bodies (if any) have completed full AI Act-specific designation, versus bodies that only have adjacent MDR/IVDR/Machinery Regulation designations.

The sources do not clarify whether the Digital Omnibus deferral (to December 2027) has been fully, finally adopted by the European Parliament and Council as binding law, or whether it remains contested in some respects as of late October 2026 — there is contradictory information on its legal status.

It is unclear how the conformity assessment deadline change interacts with harmonised standards development timelines, i.e., when such standards are expected to be finalized to support the Annex VI internal-control route.

The sources do not detail the specific competences, specializations (e.g., biometrics vs. other Annex III categories), or geographic distribution of any notified bodies that may have already been designated under the AI Act.

It is unclear how Member States' notifying authorities (e.g., Germany's Bundesnetzagentur, Ireland's arrangements) have progressed in actually notifying candidate bodies to the Commission via NANDO, as opposed to merely establishing the legal/administrative framework for doing so.

The practical timeline and process for a provider to engage a notified body (cost, duration, availability) under Annex VII is only addressed in general/estimated terms (9+ months) rather than with authoritative data.
report:
# Conformity Assessment for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act: Procedures and Notified Body Designation Status

## Executive Summary
The EU AI Act establishes two conformity assessment routes for high-risk AI systems — internal control (Annex VI) and third-party assessment via a notified body (Annex VII) — with the latter mandatory in specific circumstances such as biometric systems lacking harmonised standards ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43), high confidence). However, the pool of notified bodies actually designated for AI Act purposes remains very limited as of mid-2026, and a Commission "Digital Omnibus" proposal to delay compliance deadlines has introduced significant uncertainty about enacted versus proposed law ([governancedocs.com](https://governancedocs.com/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment); [foundational.io](https://www.foundational.io/blog/eu-ai-act-high-risk-deadline-2027)).

## Key Findings

### Conformity Assessment Procedures
Under Article 43, providers of high-risk AI systems must follow either the internal control procedure (Annex VI) or the notified-body assessment procedure (Annex VII), with Annex VII mandatory where harmonised standards do not exist, are only partially complied with, or for Annex III point 1 biometric systems (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43); [euaiact.com](https://www.euaiact.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment); [artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43)). For biometric systems specifically, providers may choose between Annex VI and Annex VII (high confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/sk/ai-act/article-43); [ba-copilot.com](https://ba-copilot.com/eu-ai-act-architecture)). Under the Annex VII route, providers may generally select any notified body, except where systems are intended for use by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions, in which case the relevant market surveillance authority performs the notified-body role (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). The Act also permits delegated acts under Article 43(5) to update Annexes VI and VII for technical progress, though this claim rests on limited sourcing (low confidence) ([fpf.org](https://fpf.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/OT-comformity-assessment-under-the-eu-ai-act-WP-1.pdf)).

### Notification and Designation Framework
Chapter III, Section 4 (Articles 28–35) establishes the notification and designation system for conformity assessment bodies, covering notifying authorities, application procedures, operational requirements, and identification numbers (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-31); [AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-30)). Designated bodies are tracked via the Commission's NANDO database, the authoritative register for notified bodies across EU product legislation (high confidence) ([NANDO](https://ec.europa.eu/growth/tools-databases/nando); [eur-lex.europa.eu](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=OJ%3AL_202402847)).

### Current Designation Status
As of early-to-mid 2026, very few notified bodies have been formally designated specifically for AI Act assessment; bodies already notified under other regimes (e.g., Medical Device Regulation, Machinery Regulation) can assess AI components within their existing scope, but dedicated AI Act designation remains scarce (low confidence) ([eyreact.com](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act); [governancedocs.com](https://governancedocs.com/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). By September 2026, the notified-body pool was still forming, with providers advised to engage candidates early given lead-time concerns comparable to ISO/IEC 42001 certification delays (low confidence) ([governancedocs.com](https://governancedocs.com/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)). Commentary draws parallels to capacity bottlenecks seen after MDR/IVDR rollout (low confidence) ([superkind.ai](https://superkind.ai/ai-lexicon/notified-body)). At national level, Germany's draft KI-MIG law designates the Bundesnetzagentur as notifying authority, with TÜV and DEKRA entities expected to seek designation (low confidence) ([superkind.ai](https://superkind.ai/ai-lexicon/notified-body)), while Ireland has designated 15 bodies as market surveillance authorities under a decentralised model, with a National AI Office planned by 2 August 2026 (medium confidence) ([artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/national-implementation-plans); [enterprise.gov.ie](https://enterprise.gov.ie/en/what-we-do/innovation-research-development/artificial-intelligence/eu-ai-act)). Council documents discuss facilitating notified-body designation for systems also covered by medical device regulations, referencing existing NANDO codes (medium confidence) ([data.consilium.europa.eu](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/WK-3257-2026-INIT/en/pdf)), and proposed amendments would empower the AI Office regarding NANDO operations (medium confidence) ([data.consilium.europa.eu](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-15708-2025-INIT/en/pdf)).

### Timeline and Digital Omnibus Changes
The original deadline for Annex III high-risk obligations, including conformity assessment, was 2 August 2026 (low confidence) ([aisecurityplatform.com](https://aisecurityplatform.com/guides/eu-ai-act-compliance-roadmap)). The Commission's November 2025 Digital Omnibus proposed deferring this to 2 December 2027, citing delayed harmonised standards and insufficient notified-body capacity (medium confidence) ([regulation-ai.eu](https://www.regulation-ai.eu/en/omnibus); [foundational.io](https://www.foundational.io/blog/eu-ai-act-high-risk-deadline-2027)). Some sources report this became binding law around July 2026 (low confidence) ([foundational.io](https://www.foundational.io/blog/eu-ai-act-high-risk-deadline-2027); [jdsupra.com](https://www.jdsupra.com/legalnews/digital-ai-omnibus-delays-key-deadlines-1900131)), while another treats it as still unenacted, advising reliance on the original August 2026 date (low confidence) ([cloudsecurityalliance.org](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-eu-ai-act-high-risk-compliance-deadline-20)). A related provision allows conformity assessment bodies to apply for AI Act designation during an 18-month window starting 27 July 2026 (medium confidence) ([artificialintelligenceact.eu](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/ai-act-explorer/digital-omnibus)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
Sources directly conflict on whether the Digital Omnibus delay is enacted law or still proposed — flagged above as low confidence on both sides. Similarly, the "choice" of assessment route for biometric systems may be illusory in practice if harmonised standards remain unavailable, forcing the Annex VII route. Several low-confidence claims (notified body designation status, German/national progress, delegated acts) warrant caution given thin sourcing.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source provides a definitive, current NANDO-based list of AI Act-specific notified bodies. It remains unclear how many bodies have completed full AI Act designation versus holding only adjacent MDR/Machinery designations, the final legal status of the Digital Omnibus deferral, and practical timelines/costs for engaging notified bodies.

This report was produced by an automated research pipeline: web search, source classification, confidence scores computed from source authority, recency and corroboration, and an automated review against the extracted claims.
